opening.headline: The problem of having “concise” and “detailed” written together to give an answer goes back and forth is solved by finding and resolving conflicts in the guidelines.
body: Line 3 of the instructions says, “Answer concisely,” and line 17 says, “Explanations are always detailed.” Each is a reasonable rule, but together there is no telling which one to follow. You become an assistant who answers the same question in two lines on some days and ten lines on other days.

In this lesson, we will first look at the structure where instruction conflicts cause malfunction. Next, you learn reading order to find conflicting rule pairs, and three resolution methods: prioritization, conditional rules, and merging. At the end, we solve the case of correcting the conflict between “Ask if you don’t know” and “Always answer” and determine whether the correction was successful.

visual.alt: A scene where two responses of different lengths alternate under one sheet of guidance document.

paragraphs: Line 3 of the assistant's instructions says "Be concise in your answers," and line 17 says "Always be detailed in your explanations." Even if you ask the same question, some days you get an answer in two lines, and other days you get an answer in ten lines.

Both rules are each reasonable. But when you're together, you can't decide which side to follow. After the person in charge changed the guidelines, we also received reports that things went wrong in other places.
The question for this class is this. How do we find and resolve conflicts?

screens.outro: First, let me recall your experience.

screens.title: Have you ever changed the instructions but found something strange elsewhere?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think first before clicking.

items.prompt: Has changing one line ever changed the response in a completely different situation?
items.answer: Guidelines apply to all conversations, so changing a single line can impact situations you didn't intend. It is easy to miss these side effects if you only check the areas that have been modified. So this lesson covers revising and revising as a single step.

items.prompt: Have you ever just kept adding instructions for months?
items.answer: Just by adding rules, rules are accumulated in chronological order, and the rules written first and rules written later handle the same situation differently without knowing each other. Adding rules is easy, but looking at their relationships with existing rules is something you need to do separately.

items.prompt: Do you have a habit of checking whether added rules conflict with old rules?
items.answer: Most focus only on the problems the new rules are intended to solve. When writing a new rule, you can prevent many conflicts in advance by just having a habit of checking to see if there are already other rules in the situation that this rule touches.

screens.outro: Now that we have summarized our experience, let us first look at the structure in which collisions lead to malfunctions.

screens.title: Structure where instruction conflict causes malfunction
screens.lead: Click the Next Step button to follow a question as it passes through two conflicting rules and diverges into different responses.

visual.alt: A diagram in which a question passes through two rules and is divided into different answers at a crossroads.

steps.title: definition of conflict
steps.body: Conflicting guidelines are the presence of rules that require opposite actions in the same situation. Every single rule is correct. The problem is that both rules hang on the same situation.

steps.title: The question passes both rules
steps.body: When a user sends a question, the assistant tries to follow all the rules in the instructions. This question applies both the rule of brevity and the rule of detail. There is no response that satisfies both rules simultaneously.

steps.title: Answers vary at a crossroads
steps.body: If they cannot be satisfied at the same time, the assistant will choose one side for each situation. In some conversations, brevity wins, and in others, detail wins. So the answers come and go, and it is difficult to guess the cause.

steps.title: Conflicts caused by range differences
steps.body: Conflict is not just about apparent opposites. The rule to always answer and the rule to ask if you don't know are not opposites, but they require opposite actions in questions that lack information. Where the coverage of rules overlaps is a point of conflict.

steps.title: A single line of contradiction spreads through every conversation.
steps.body: GPT guidance explains that the guidelines apply to all conversations, guiding tone, structure, and judgment. Therefore, even a single line of contradiction in the instructions spreads into every conversation. Before blaming the model for a malfunction, it is important to first suspect contradictions in the instructions.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the structure, let's see how to actually find conflicting rule pairs.

screens.title: Spotting conflict rules: reading order and notation
screens.lead: Please select one by one the passages highlighted in the full instructions below. An explanation appears as to which pair of rules is being hit and why.

data.text:
[Consultation Assistant Guidelines Expert]
1. Respond to customers using polite language.
3. Write your answer concisely.
5. Always provide answers to any questions.
8. If information is insufficient, ask the user.
12. Refund policies must be provided in the original text.
15. Explain complex terms in simple language so that users can easily understand.
17. Always write detailed explanations.
20. Never guess and answer.

marks.note: The action verb is to write and the direction is to reduce. We are in the same situation as detailed in line 17, so actions in opposite directions are paired. The process involves underlining the verbs in step 1 and finding pairs of opposite directions in step 2.
This is a rule that pairs with line 3. Since it has the absolute word always, it is also a rule to be checked first in step 3. Absolute rules allow no exceptions and are therefore prone to conflict.

marks.span: 5. Always provide answers to any questions.
marks.note: The rule is to answer all questions. Line 8 clashes with a follow-up question and a question that lacks information. Even if the words are not opposites, if their scopes overlap, they result in conflict.

marks.span: 8. If information is insufficient, ask the user.
marks.note: Matches line 5. Line 5 tells you to answer questions that lack information, and line 8 tells you to ask back. Unless the instructions state which of the two rules comes first, the other is chosen for each conversation.

It also clashes with the always answer in line 5. Because there is no way to answer a question you don't know without guessing. If there is more than one rule using absolute language, be suspicious first.

marks.span: 12. Refund policies must be provided in the original text.
marks.note: The difficult words in line 15 may conflict with the rule to explain. The original and unpacked explanations call for the opposite action in the same refund instructions. You can spot conflicts by examining both the reason and scope of the rule.

screens.outro: Once you've found the conflict, let's look at three ways to resolve it.

screens.title: Solutions: Prioritization, conditional rules, merging
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare fixes made by all three methods to the same conflict pair.

tabs.label: specify priorities
tabs.body: This is a method of writing down in sentences which side is ahead when rules conflict. Write down the order, for example, “If there is a conflict, the accuracy of the refund instructions takes precedence over the rules of speech.” It leaves both rules but provides a judgment standard in case of conflict, so it is appropriate when both rules are absolutely necessary but the order is not determined. When writing down the order, it is a good idea to add a line explaining why it is in that order. Claude Guidance explains that if you write down the reason for your guidance, the assistant will better reflect your intent.

tabs.label: conditional rule
tabs.body: This is a method of narrowing the scope of application by adding conditions to the rule. Conflict between concise and detailed should be replaced with "If the question is simple, answer in two lines. If the user asks for more detail, explain step by step." Now the two rules hit different situations and don't collide. GPT guidance recommends an explicit step-by-step structure and positive instructions for what to do if something happens. Conditional rules are the closest resolution to this recommendation.

tabs.label: Merge
tabs.body: This is a method of combining two overlapping lines into one sentence to eliminate the possibility of contradiction. For example, put both intentions in one sentence, such as “Write the answer in one paragraph starting from the main point, and add evidence only when the user requests it.” The assistant doesn't have to choose between two rules because you've already decided the balance within a sentence. This is especially appropriate when two rules actually express the same intent in different ways.

tabs.label: Criteria for choosing
tabs.body: Choose one of the three methods depending on the situation. If both rules are important and only the order matters, use a priority rule, if the situations in which they apply are different, use a conditional rule, and if the same intent is written twice, use a merge rule. Either way, you must preview it after making any changes. We encourage you to add prompts to the Gemini Gems guide preview and edit the instructions.

screens.outro: Now that you have learned the method, let's solve an actual collision case with the instructor.

screens.title: Commentary: Adjust “Ask if you don’t know” and “Always answer”
screens.lead: Click the Next Step button to follow the process of turning two conflicting rules into one flow.

visual.alt: The process by which two conflicting rules become one flow by obtaining conditions and order.
labels: If you don't know, ask the user
Always provide answers to any questions
Is there a lack of information?

steps.title: Conflict Check
steps.body: The guidelines include “If you don’t know, ask the user” and “Always provide an answer to any question.” There is no problem if you ask enough questions, but in questions that lack information, one rule says to ask back and another rule says to answer. So some days I ask questions, and other days I guess and answer.

steps.title: Step 1: Determine the Confronting Situation
steps.body: First, write down in words the exact situation in which the two rules collide. In this case, the question is lacking information. In well-informed questions, the two rules do not conflict. Once you define the situation, the scope to resolve narrows down.

steps.title: Step 2: Convert to a conditional rule
steps.body: Turn it into a rule that applies only when questions are lacking information. It is a pair of condition and action: "If there is insufficient information, ask again for the necessary items. If there is still no information, state the assumption and answer." Always answering remains the rule when information is sufficient.

steps.title: Step 3: State your priorities
steps.body: If you don't decide how many times to ask back, new problems arise from endless questions. So, I write down the order as follows: “Ask a question only once, and after that, the answer comes first.” It would be a good idea to add a reason as well. The reason is to avoid a situation where the user only receives questions without receiving an answer.

steps.title: Instructions after modification
steps.body: After revision, it becomes one flow: “Ask once, and if you still don’t know, state your assumptions and answer.” The two rules are no longer opposites, but have become back-and-forth steps. The no-guessing rules are also put together in a way that reveals assumptions.

screens.outro: Now that we've fixed it, let's see how to determine if this fix really resolved the crash.

screens.title: Commentary: Re-confirmation and resolution decision after revision
screens.lead: The table below shows how we revisit revised guidelines and determine whether they should be resolved. Read each line from left to right.

data.caption: Re-confirmation procedure and judgment criteria after modification
rows: Put conflicting question types back into the preview, i.e. questions with insufficient information.
Even if the same question is asked twice, do you ask it again in the same way and then answer by stating your hypothesis?
Also include question types unrelated to editing, i.e. information questions and refund information questions.
Is the response the same as before except for the areas that have been modified?
Leave the version before modification and revert to the previous version if a problem occurs.
Can I review and revert to previous versions?
Collect the previous three results to determine whether or not to resolve
If all are met, it is considered resolved, otherwise the priorities or conditions are further specified.
data.notes: GPT instructions explain that changes are saved as drafts, and version history allows you to review and revert to previous versions. If you are not confident in your corrections, you can try it safely using this feature. When determining resolution, it is important to ask the same question multiple times to see if the responses are consistent. With just one check, you won't be able to tell the difference between an accidental hit and a regular hit. If the decision is ambiguous, add another question type and compare the answers. If it is still inconsistent, refine the rule conditions to be more specific.

screens.outro: Now that I've finished rechecking, I'll summarize the main points of this class.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarizes the contents of this class. As you read, try to answer the opening question: How do we find and resolve conflict?

paragraphs: The initial question was how to find and resolve conflicts. Malfunctions usually occur not because the model is unstable, but because the instructions contain rules that require opposite actions in the same situation. This is because the assistant will try to follow all the rules, and if it cannot be satisfied at the same time, it will pick a side in each situation.

When looking for conflicts, underline the action verb for each rule and look for pairs of opposite verbs in the same situation. First, we check rules with absolute words such as always, never, and always, then pick one misbehaving response and trace back which rule was followed and which rule was broken.

There are three solutions. These include specifying priorities to write down the order, conditional rules to attach conditions to situations, and merging to combine two overlapping lines into one sentence. After making corrections, you must re-check both the areas that have been fixed and those that have not been fixed to prevent side effects.

Recall the rules from the first scene succinctly and in detail. The two rules can be used together without conflict, with one conditional rule: if the question is simple, answer in two lines, and if a detailed request is asked, answer step-by-step. Attaching conditions and reasons to rules like this applies equally to ChatGPT's GPT and project, Claude project, and Gem's instructions.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: After changing the instructions, don't just look at the areas that have been changed, but also check the areas that haven't been changed. Because the guidelines apply to all conversations. Even when adding a new rule, if you get into the habit of checking first to see if there are already other rules for the same situation, you can prevent most conflicts at the moment of writing.

glossary.def: A situation where there are rules that require opposite actions in the same situation. When conflict occurs, responses waver from situation to situation.
When rules collide, which side takes precedence is determined in a sentence.
It is a rule that narrows the scope of application to a certain action in a certain situation.
This is the process of revising the instructions and then checking the preview to see what has been changed and what has not been changed.

misconceptions.myth: The reason the response fluctuates is because the model is unstable.
misconceptions.fact: First, look for opposing rules within the guidelines. If there are conflicting rules, your assistant will pick a different side in each situation.

misconceptions.myth: Conflicts only occur when there are opposite words.
misconceptions.fact: Even if the words are not opposites, they clash when their scope of application overlaps. Examples include always answering and asking when you don't know.

misconceptions.myth: If you change just one line, only that part changes.
misconceptions.fact: The guidelines apply to all conversations, so you'll need to double-check what you've fixed and what you haven't.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Malfunctions are usually the result of conflicting instructions.
Look for conflicts in pairs with opposite action verbs and in rules with absolute words.
Resolve conflicts by specifying priorities, conditional rules, and merging.
After making modifications, check again all areas that have been modified and those that are different.
